edges.description: Absorbed methanol is oxidized by hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase.
Methanol itself produces mild central nervous system depression before metabolism.
Formaldehyde is rapidly oxidized to formate.
Formate is produced faster than it is eliminated and accumulates.
Accumulated formate inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase.
edges.target: Cytochrome c oxidase inhibition by formate

edges.description: Accumulated formate is a major unmeasured anion contributing to the acidosis.
Formate is directly toxic to the retina and optic nerve.
Impaired oxidative phosphorylation forces anaerobic metabolism and lactate production.
edges.source: Cytochrome c oxidase inhibition by formate

edges.description: Mitochondrial dysfunction from Complex IV inhibition generates reactive oxygen species and drives apoptotic cell death.
edges.source: Cytochrome c oxidase inhibition by formate

edges.description: Oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation amplify the optic nerve and retinal injury.
Oxidative injury contributes to basal-ganglia neuronal death.
Lactate accumulation from anaerobic metabolism contributes to the high anion gap acidosis.
Energy failure in the metabolically demanding basal ganglia produces putaminal necrosis.
Severe acidosis and systemic toxicity depress the central nervous system.
Methanol-adulterated or illicitly distilled spirits are swallowed as if they were drinking alcohol, delivering a methanol dose orally.
These household fluids are ingested, often as an ethanol substitute, delivering methanol by the same oral route.

An uncommon, non-oral route: occupational methanol vapour or skin contact can load methanol systemically without any ingestion. Almost all clinical poisoning is oral, so this route is documented but rare.

nodes.description: Drinking methanol-adulterated or illicitly distilled spirits, including homemade alcoholic beverages, is the leading cause of methanol poisoning outbreaks worldwide.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical presentation and management of methanol poisoning outbreaks in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia: a retrospective analysis.
evidence.snippet: Homemade alcoholic beverages are a frequent source of such poisoning.

nodes.description: Hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) oxidizes methanol to formaldehyde. This is the rate-limiting step and the target of antidotal therapy with fomepizole and ethanol.

evidence.reference_title: American Academy of Clinical Toxicology practice guidelines on the treatment of methanol poisoning.
evidence.snippet: Methanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde.

nodes.description: Formaldehyde is very rapidly oxidized by aldehyde/formaldehyde dehydrogenase to formic acid (formate); because this step is fast, formaldehyde does not accumulate.

evidence.reference_title: American Academy of Clinical Toxicology practice guidelines on the treatment of methanol poisoning.
evidence.snippet: The oxidation of formaldehyde to formic acid is facilitated by formaldehyde dehydrogenase.

nodes.description: Formate toxicity and energy failure produce bilateral putaminal necrosis, at times hemorrhagic, the substrate for delayed parkinsonism and dystonia in survivors.

evidence.reference_title: Importance of Susceptibility-weighted-imaging in Methanol Toxicity.
evidence.snippet: Haemorrhagic necrosis of bilateral basal ganglia, particularly of the putamen, is one of the distinctive features of this entity.

nodes.description: Inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation depletes cellular ATP and shifts metabolism toward anaerobic glycolysis, generating lactate that adds to the acidosis and injuring metabolically demanding tissues such as the basal ganglia.

evidence.reference_title: Approach to the Treatment of Methanol Intoxication.
evidence.snippet: Its adverse effects are due primarily to the impact of its major metabolite formic acid and lactic acid resulting from cellular hypoxia.

nodes.description: Methanol itself and the ensuing acidosis and histotoxic hypoxia depress the central nervous system, producing inebriation, confusion, decreased consciousness, coma, and, in severe poisoning, seizures.

evidence.reference_title: Delayed neurological sequelae from ethylene glycol, diethylene glycol and methanol poisonings.
evidence.snippet: patients frequently develop an early neurological syndrome consisting of inebriation, ataxia, and if severe, seizures and coma.

nodes.description: Formate binds and inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), impairing oxidative phosphorylation and producing histotoxic (cellular) hypoxia independent of oxygen delivery, and is the prime cause of the ocular toxicity.
nodes.id: Cytochrome c oxidase inhibition by formate

biological_processes: mitochondrial electron transport, cytochrome c to oxygen

evidence.reference_title: American Academy of Clinical Toxicology practice guidelines on the treatment of methanol poisoning.
evidence.snippet: Formic acid has also been shown to inhibit cytochrome oxidase and is the prime cause of ocular toxicity, though acidosis can increase toxicity further by enabling greater diffusion of formic acid into cells.

nodes.description: Ethanol competes with methanol for alcohol dehydrogenase and can be used to block methanol metabolism when fomepizole is unavailable.

evidence.snippet: administration of enteral or parenteral ethanol to competitively inhibit the metabolic breakdown of methanol to formic acid.

nodes.description: Folinic acid (or folic acid) accelerates the folate-dependent oxidation of formate to carbon dioxide by 10-formyltetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase (ALDH1L1/FDH), enhancing clearance of the toxic metabolite.

evidence.snippet: administration of folic acid may be of benefit by hastening the metabolism of formic acid to carbon dioxide.

nodes.description: Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase that blocks conversion of methanol to formate, halting toxin production; it is the preferred antidote.

evidence.reference_title: Fomepizole for the treatment of methanol poisoning.
evidence.snippet: In response to fomepizole, plasma formic acid concentrations fell and metabolic abnormalities resolved in all patients.

nodes.description: Formate is eliminated slowly because its folate-dependent conversion to carbon dioxide by 10-formyltetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase (ALDH1L1/FDH) is rate-limited and saturable in humans, so it accumulates and is the proximate toxin responsible for the metabolic, ocular, and neurological injury. This slow, folate-dependent clearance is the rationale for folinic-acid rescue.

evidence.reference_title: American Academy of Clinical Toxicology practice guidelines on the treatment of methanol poisoning.
evidence.snippet: In cases of methanol poisoning, formic acid accumulates and there is a direct correlation between the formic acid concentration and increased morbidity and mortality.

nodes.description: Hemodialysis removes methanol and formate and corrects the metabolic acidosis, and is used in severe poisoning with acidosis, visual symptoms, or high methanol concentrations.

evidence.snippet: Hemodialysis accelerates the elimination of both methanol and formic acid and also assists in correction of the metabolic acidosis.

nodes.description: Accumulated formate and lactate produce a severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis; the low pH increases the proportion of undissociated formic acid, which crosses membranes more readily and worsens cellular toxicity in a feed-forward loop.

evidence.reference_title: American Academy of Clinical Toxicology practice guidelines on the treatment of methanol poisoning.
evidence.snippet: The acidosis observed in methanol poisoning appears to be caused directly or indirectly by formic acid production.

nodes.description: Occupational or accidental exposure to methanol-containing industrial solvents, fuels, and cleaning products can cause poisoning, rarely by inhalation or dermal absorption.

evidence.reference_title: American Academy of Clinical Toxicology practice guidelines on the treatment of methanol poisoning.
evidence.snippet: Almost all cases of acute methanol toxicity result from ingestion, though rarely cases of poisoning have followed inhalation or dermal absorption.

nodes.description: Methanol is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, with peak concentrations within 30-60 minutes, and distributed in body water. Methanol itself is only mildly intoxicating; toxicity requires its metabolism to formic acid.

evidence.reference_title: American Academy of Clinical Toxicology practice guidelines on the treatment of methanol poisoning.
evidence.snippet: The absorption of methanol following oral administration is rapid and peak methanol concentrations occur within 30-60minutes.

nodes.description: Beyond direct Complex IV inhibition, formate toxicity intensifies oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation with formation of cytotoxic compounds and apoptotic cell death, amplifying tissue injury in the optic nerve, retina, and basal ganglia.

evidence.reference_title: Methanol-induced optic neuropathy: a still-present problem.
evidence.snippet: damage to the eye tissues by oxidative stress causing the intensification of the oxidative peroxidation process with the formation of cytotoxic compounds

nodes.description: Formate inhibits mitochondrial respiration in retinal ganglion cells and the optic nerve head, producing optic disc edema, optic neuropathy, and visual loss that can become permanent blindness.

evidence.reference_title: Delayed neurological sequelae from ethylene glycol, diethylene glycol and methanol poisonings.
evidence.snippet: Formic acid is implicated in the optic nerve damage associated with methanol.

nodes.description: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate corrects the metabolic acidosis and, by raising pH, shifts formate toward its ionized form that penetrates tissues less readily.

evidence.snippet: correction of the metabolic acidosis with sodium bicarbonate

nodes.description: Ingestion of methanol-containing windshield washer fluid or antifreeze, often as an ethanol substitute, is a common source.

evidence.reference_title: Delayed neurological sequelae from ethylene glycol, diethylene glycol and methanol poisonings.
evidence.snippet: are found in a variety of common household products including antifreeze, windshield washer fluid, brake fluid and lubricants.
